title: Confirmation Bias (Part 1)
hook: A tidy incident timeline can make the missing calls look less important than the calls that fit.
coreIdea: Once a conclusion feels plausible, confirmation bias makes supporting evidence easier to notice and disconfirming evidence easier to explain away.
counterintuition: Good evidence hunting often feels backwards: you protect a promising idea by trying to wound it. The danger is not confidence itself; it is letting one early conclusion decide which facts are allowed to matter.
tryThisNow: Pick one current belief and write one sentence that would weaken it if true. Then look for that sentence before collecting more support.
keyTakeaway: Before you trust the evidence that agrees with you, ask what would have to be true for your view to be wrong.

breakdown.fastRead:
A tidy incident timeline sits in the dispatch room with every delayed ambulance call highlighted in yellow. Daniel sees the pattern he expected: the new triage script is slowing the team. Then a supervisor points to the blank left column where faster calls were never logged.

Confirmation bias begins after a view has already taken shape. Your attention becomes a customs officer. Supporting facts pass easily. Disconfirming evidence gets delayed, questioned, or treated as a special case.

The fix is not to become doubtful about everything.

It is to ask, before deciding, what fact would count against the current explanation and where that fact would be visible.
breakdown.deepRead:
The incident timeline in Daniel's dispatch office looks convincing because it has color, sequence, and urgency. Every slow response is easy to see. Every normal response is absent. If the team decides from that sheet, they are not judging the triage script; they are judging the part of the script that already fits the complaint.

Confirmation bias is selective admission. It does not need you to lie. It only needs you to search unevenly. You ask the unhappy crews for examples and forget to ask the crews whose nights improved. You remember the one call where the script sounded clumsy and forget the ten calls where it forced the right question early. A fixed conclusion turns evidence into a supporting cast.

Disconfirming evidence is not an enemy; it is the missing door.

A useful test is simple: if my explanation were wrong, what would I expect to see? Daniel adds a second column to the timeline: calls that became faster after the script. He asks the shift lead to pull both kinds before the review. The point is not to save the script. The point is to stop the complaint from choosing the sample.

A travel insurance pricing desk faces the same problem in a quieter form. Megan sees a warranty label that says adventure coverage and assumes the costly claims must come from mountain trips. Her analyst finds a cheaper pattern in missed ferry connections. Megan circles disconfirming evidence on the warranty label and delays the rate change until the ferry claims sit beside the climbing claims.

Support is cheap when you only invite supporters.
breakdown.fullRead:
Static crackles through the podcast studio monitor while Ivo rereads a press clipping about a host's sold-out live show. The clipping feels like proof that renewing the ad buy is obvious. The producer smiles. The sponsor wants another six months. Ivo has one problem: the download report is open beside the clipping, and the ad code has been flat for eight weeks.

Confirmation bias loves mixed evidence because mixed evidence gives it room to choose. The press clipping is vivid. The download report is dull. The live show feels public and impressive. The ad code feels like a spreadsheet muttering in the corner. If Ivo already wants the renewal, the clipping becomes a signal and the report becomes noise.

The Wason test made this habit visible in miniature: people tend to check the cards that might confirm a rule instead of the cards that could break it. That small laboratory pattern has a daily business version. You test the happy case first. You ask the friendly customer. You search for the number that would make the pitch look sensible. Then you call the answer balanced because you found evidence.

What would you check if your favorite answer were false?

Charles Darwin had a practical defense against this pull. When a fact damaged one of his ideas, he tried to write it down quickly because he knew the mind would forget what it did not want. That habit matters because disconfirming evidence often arrives without drama. It is a quiet exception, a low response rate, a missing comparison group, a customer who left without complaining.

You do not need a grand theory to use the move. Before Ivo renews the podcast ad, he writes two tests on the press clipping. First, which metric would make renewal look weak? Second, where is that metric already recorded? Then he asks the producer to compare ad-code redemptions with two other channels. The clipping can stay in the file. It just cannot be the file.

A university lab result meeting shows the danger more sharply. You have a voting sheet in front of you, and the principal investigator wants to call the trial promising. The early responders look good. The dropout notes look messy. A junior researcher, Hadiya, marks fixed conclusion at the top of the sheet before the vote and asks for the dropout reasons to be read aloud. The room goes quiet because the missing evidence is no longer missing.

This is the uncomfortable part: the best question may make your preferred answer less clean.

That discomfort is useful. Confirmation bias feels smooth because each added fact agrees with the direction you were already moving. Disconfirming evidence creates friction. It slows the story down. It asks whether the conclusion earned its confidence or merely collected flattering witnesses.

So keep a rule for serious choices. Do not ask only, what supports this? Ask, what would change my mind, and have I looked where that evidence would live? Until that second question has a real answer, the evidence is still being screened by the conclusion.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Confirmation bias turns a first answer into a filter. Decisions improve when the reader knows how to force the missing comparison before support becomes a story.

examples.whyItMatters: A promising result can be real and still incomplete. Confirmation bias hides in the facts the room is relieved not to discuss.

examples.whatToDo: Use the inventory scan from the decision time, not the scan that confirmed the morning assumption. Update the map from the evidence that could have contradicted it.
examples.whyItMatters: Confirmation can freeze an early status into a plan. The postmortem protects the next heat response by asking where the contrary evidence would have appeared.

reviewCards.front: A report supports your first explanation, but one column that might weaken it is blank. What should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask what evidence would count against the explanation and where that evidence would appear. Fill that column before deciding.

reviewCards.front: A team keeps finding examples that prove its plan is working. What is the confirmation-bias warning sign?
reviewCards.back: The search may be tilted toward support. Look for the cases that would break the plan's story, not only the cases that flatter it.

reviewCards.front: A colleague calls contrary evidence a distraction. What is the better frame?
reviewCards.back: Disconfirming evidence is the missing door. It tests whether the conclusion earned confidence or merely recruited friendly facts.

reviewCards.front: You like a proposal and want to approve it quickly. What one sentence should you write first?
reviewCards.back: Write: 'This proposal would look weak if...' Then check whether that condition is already visible in the evidence.

reviewCards.front: A vivid story and a dull spreadsheet disagree. Which one deserves attention?
reviewCards.back: Both, but the dull spreadsheet may be the disconfirming evidence your preferred story wants to ignore.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to test a favored answer by naming the evidence that would weaken it, then checking where that evidence should appear before the decision closes.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I notice myself collecting only examples that support my current view, then I will write the opposite evidence I would expect to see and check one source where it should appear.
If a meeting starts with a favored conclusion already named, then I will ask for the strongest fact that would weaken that conclusion before the group votes.
If a dashboard number confirms what I hoped was true, then I will look for one comparison period, group, or channel that could explain the same number another way.
If someone dismisses a contrary case as an exception, then I will ask whether we have counted how many similar exceptions exist before treating it as harmless.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one belief you are using to make a decision. Write the one fact that would weaken it, then spend five minutes looking for that fact before collecting more support.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, revisit a decision you feel sure about and add a disconfirming-evidence column before you act on it.
